title: A New Neighbour
summaryVi: Lan giúp người hàng xóm mới tên Tom chuyển đồ vào căn hộ, và hai người trở thành bạn.
body:
Lan is twenty-two years old. She lives in a small flat in a big city. Her flat is on the fifth floor. It has one bedroom, a little kitchen and a window with a view of the park.

One Saturday morning, Lan hears a noise in the hall. She opens the door. A young man is carrying a lot of boxes. He looks tired. “Hello,” Lan says. “Do you need help?” The man smiles. “Yes, please! I'm Tom. I'm your new neighbour.”

Lan and Tom carry the boxes into his flat. There are books, plates, a lamp and a guitar. After an hour, they are both hungry. Tom makes two cups of tea, and Lan brings some bread and fruit from her kitchen. They sit on the floor and eat.

Tom is a music teacher. Lan is a nurse. In the evening, Tom plays the guitar. Lan listens from her window and smiles. The building feels friendly now.

title: The Red Umbrella
summaryVi: Mai bỏ quên chiếc ô đỏ trên xe buýt. Sáng hôm sau, một ông lão hàng xóm mang ô trả lại và hai người trở thành bạn.
body:
It was raining hard when Mai left the office on Friday evening. She opened her old red umbrella and walked to the bus stop. The bus was late, so she waited under the roof with a group of students and an elderly man in a grey coat.

When the bus finally arrived, everyone hurried on. Mai found a seat at the back and closed her eyes for a few minutes. She was very tired after a long week. Suddenly she heard the driver call the name of her stop, and she jumped off quickly.

When she got to her apartment, she noticed a problem: her umbrella was still on the bus. She felt annoyed, but it was just an umbrella, so she decided to forget about it.

The next morning, someone knocked on her door. It was the elderly man from the bus stop. He was holding her red umbrella. “I saw you leave it on your seat,” he explained. “I live in the building opposite yours, so I recognised you.”

Mai thanked him and invited him in for coffee. His name was Mr Harris, and he had lived in the neighbourhood for forty years. He told her funny stories about the street when it was full of small shops. Since that day, they have met for coffee every Saturday.

title: Breakfast Around the World
summaryVi: Bài viết giới thiệu bữa sáng ở Việt Nam, Anh, Nhật Bản và Mexico.
body:
People eat different breakfasts in different countries. Let's look at four of them.

In Vietnam, many people eat a hot bowl of noodle soup in the morning. Some people buy it from a small shop near their home. Others like sticky rice or a bread roll with meat and vegetables.

In England, a traditional breakfast is very big. It has eggs, bacon, sausages, beans, tomatoes and toast. But most English people only eat this at the weekend. On weekdays, they often have cereal with milk or a slice of toast.

In Japan, breakfast is often rice, fish, miso soup and vegetables. It is healthy and light.

In Mexico, some people eat eggs with tortillas, beans and a spicy sauce.

What do you eat for breakfast? Is it sweet or salty? Is it hot or cold? Breakfast is important because it gives us energy for the day.

title: Why We Should Walk More
summaryVi: Bài viết giải thích lợi ích của việc đi bộ đối với cơ thể và tinh thần, những khó khăn khi đi bộ ở thành phố và mục tiêu 30 phút mỗi ngày.
body:
For most of human history, walking was simply how people got from one place to another. Today, many of us spend the whole day sitting: at a desk, in a car or in front of a screen. Health experts say that this change has a real cost, and that one of the easiest ways to improve our health is also one of the oldest: walking.

Regular walking strengthens the heart and lungs, helps to control weight and reduces the risk of several serious illnesses. It is also good for the mind. Many people find that a short walk helps them to calm down after a stressful day or to think more clearly about a problem. Some writers say that their best ideas come to them while they are walking.

One advantage of walking is that it costs nothing and requires no special equipment. You do not need to join a gym or buy expensive clothes; a comfortable pair of shoes is enough. It is also easy to include walking in daily life. You could get off the bus one stop early, take the stairs instead of the lift, or walk to the shops instead of driving.

Of course, walking is not always convenient. In some cities, the pavements are narrow or crowded, and the air can be polluted. In very hot or rainy weather, people naturally prefer to stay indoors. City planners can help by creating safer routes, planting more trees and building green spaces.

Experts often suggest a goal of around thirty minutes of walking a day. This does not have to happen all at once; three ten-minute walks can be just as useful. The most important thing is to start, and then to keep going.

title: Town Library Starts Lending Tools and Games
summaryVi: (Tin hư cấu) Thư viện ở thị trấn Greenfield bắt đầu cho mượn đồ dùng như máy khoan, lều, trò chơi – ý tưởng đến từ nhóm học sinh địa phương.
body:
GREENFIELD — The public library in the small town of Greenfield has started lending something new: not books, but things.

Since Monday, library members can borrow more than two hundred useful items, including drills, sewing machines, camping tents, board games and even a karaoke machine. Members can keep each item for up to one week, and borrowing is free.

The idea came from a group of local teenagers. “Lots of people buy a tool, use it once and then keep it in a cupboard for years,” said one of the students, sixteen-year-old Ella. “We thought it was a waste of money and space.”

The library asked residents to donate things they no longer needed. In just three weeks, people gave more than three hundred items. Volunteers checked every item to make sure it was clean and safe.

On the first day, over ninety items were borrowed. The most popular was a ladder, followed by a pasta maker.

The head librarian, David Okafor, said he was delighted. “A library is about sharing,” he said. “Sharing things is a natural next step.” The library now plans to offer short workshops so that people can learn how to use some of the tools safely.

title: City Turns Rooftops into Gardens
summaryVi: (Tin hư cấu) Thành phố Port Allard hỗ trợ tiền để biến mái nhà thành vườn. Bài nêu lợi ích (chống ngập, làm mát, giáo dục) và những ý kiến phản đối.
body:
PORT ALLARD — Look up in the centre of Port Allard this summer and you might see tomatoes, sunflowers and even beehives. Over the past two years, more than forty office buildings and schools in this coastal city have turned their flat rooftops into gardens as part of a city programme called Green Roofs.

The programme offers building owners a grant that covers up to half of the cost of creating a roof garden. In return, owners must keep the garden for at least ten years and open it to the public or to local schools at least once a month.

Supporters say the benefits are clear. Plants absorb rainwater, which reduces the risk of flooding in the streets below. They also keep buildings cooler in summer, so less energy is needed for air conditioning. According to the city council, the surface of a typical green roof is several degrees cooler than a traditional roof on a hot afternoon.

The gardens have social benefits, too. At Harbour Street Primary School, pupils grow vegetables on the roof and use them in cooking lessons. “Children who never ate salad now ask for more, because they grew it themselves,” said teacher Rosa Lindqvist.

However, not everyone is enthusiastic. Some engineers warn that older buildings may not be strong enough to carry the extra weight of soil and water, so every roof must be inspected before work begins. Others point out that the money could be spent on parks at street level, which are easier for elderly and disabled people to reach.

The council says it will publish a full report on the programme next spring. If the results are positive, the scheme could be extended to apartment buildings.

title: Where Does Rain Come From?
summaryVi: Bài giải thích vòng tuần hoàn của nước: mặt trời làm nước bốc hơi, hơi nước tạo thành mây, rồi mưa rơi xuống.
body:
Water is everywhere. It is in the sea, in rivers, in the clouds and even in our bodies. But where does rain come from? The answer is the water cycle.

First, the sun heats the water in seas, lakes and rivers. Some of the water turns into a gas called water vapour. The vapour goes up into the sky. We cannot see it.

High in the sky, the air is cold. The vapour becomes very small drops of water. Many small drops together make a cloud.

When the drops in a cloud get bigger and heavier, they fall to the ground. This is rain. When it is very cold, they fall as snow.

The rain goes into rivers, lakes and the sea. Then the sun heats the water again, and the cycle starts again. The same water goes around and around for millions of years. Maybe the water in your glass today was once in the sea near a dinosaur!

title: The Hidden Network Beneath the Forest
summaryVi: Rễ cây trong rừng được nối với nhau bởi mạng lưới nấm. Bài viết giải thích mối quan hệ cộng sinh này, những phát hiện gây chú ý và cuộc tranh luận khoa học xung quanh nó.
body:
Walk through a forest and you will see trees competing for light, each one stretching upwards in a silent race. Yet beneath your feet, something rather different may be happening. Scientists have discovered that the roots of many trees are connected by vast networks of fungi, and these networks appear to allow trees to exchange resources and, possibly, signals.

The relationship begins with a simple trade. Fungi produce thin threads, called hyphae, which spread through the soil and wrap around, or even enter, tree roots. These threads are far finer than roots and can reach water and minerals that the roots alone would miss. In exchange, the tree supplies the fungi with sugars that it produces through photosynthesis. This partnership, known as mycorrhiza, is extremely ancient and involves the great majority of land plants.

What surprised researchers was evidence that a single fungal network can link several trees at once, sometimes of different species. In experiments using carbon that could be traced, scientists found that carbon from one tree had travelled into its neighbours. Some studies suggested that large, older trees might send resources to seedlings growing in deep shade, improving their chances of survival. The media quickly nicknamed the system the “wood wide web”.

However, the idea has become controversial. Several ecologists have argued that popular accounts have exaggerated the findings. They point out that many experiments were carried out in laboratories or on a small scale, and that it is difficult to prove that resources are moved deliberately rather than simply leaking along the network. The claim that “mother trees” look after their offspring, they say, is an attractive story but not yet an established fact.

What is not in doubt is the importance of fungi to healthy forests. Without them, many trees would grow slowly or not at all. This has practical consequences: when forests are cleared and replanted, foresters increasingly pay attention to the soil and its fungal life, not just to the young trees above it.

The story of the forest network is also a useful lesson in how science works: an exciting discovery, followed by careful questioning, and gradually a clearer and more accurate picture.

title: Keeping Your Online Accounts Safe
summaryVi: Bài hướng dẫn cách tạo mật khẩu mạnh, dùng trình quản lý mật khẩu và bật xác minh hai bước để bảo vệ tài khoản.
body:
Today, most of us have many online accounts: email, social media, banking, shopping and more. Each account needs a password, and remembering them all is not easy. Because of this, many people use the same simple password everywhere. This is a big mistake.

If a criminal discovers your password for one website, they can try it on all your other accounts. Simple passwords like “123456” or your date of birth are also very easy to guess. Computer programs can try millions of combinations in a few seconds.

So what makes a good password? First, it should be long – at least twelve characters. A good idea is to join three or four random words together, for example “purple-lamp-river-tiger”. This is easy for you to remember but hard for a computer to guess. Second, use a different password for every important account.

You can also use a password manager. This is an app that creates strong passwords and saves them for you, so you only need to remember one main password.

Finally, turn on two-step verification when you can. With this, the website sends a code to your phone every time you log in from a new device. Even if someone knows your password, they cannot enter your account without the code.

title: Who Can Fix Your Phone?
summaryVi: Bài viết bàn về phong trào “quyền được sửa chữa”: vì sao thiết bị hiện đại khó sửa, lợi ích môi trường của việc sửa đồ, và lo ngại của các nhà sản xuất.
body:
When a smartphone screen cracks or a laptop battery stops holding its charge, many people simply buy a new device. Sometimes this is a choice, but often it is because repairing the old one is surprisingly difficult or expensive. A growing movement, often called “the right to repair”, argues that this situation needs to change.

There are several reasons why modern devices are hard to fix. Some manufacturers glue batteries in place instead of using screws, which makes them difficult to remove safely. Spare parts may only be sold to official repair centres, and repair manuals are often not available to the public. In some cases, a replacement part will not work properly unless it is approved by the company's software.

Supporters of the right to repair argue that people should be able to fix the things they own, or take them to an independent repair shop of their choice. They also point to the environmental cost of electronic waste, which is one of the fastest-growing kinds of rubbish in the world. Producing a new phone requires metals, energy and water, so keeping an old one working for an extra two or three years can make a real difference.

Manufacturers have their own concerns. They say that unofficial repairs can be unsafe, especially with batteries, and that sharing their designs could put security at risk. Some also argue that thin, waterproof devices are only possible because parts are glued together.

In recent years, a number of governments have introduced rules that require companies to make spare parts and repair information available for a certain number of years. Some companies now sell repair kits directly to customers. The debate is far from over, but it raises a simple question that affects everyone: when you buy something, how much of it do you really own?

summaryVi: Hoa bắt đầu làm bánh tại nhà, bán qua mạng xã hội, học cách quản lý chi phí và khách hàng, rồi mở được một tiệm bánh nhỏ.
body:
Three years ago, Hoa started baking cakes in her small kitchen at home. At first, she only made them for friends and family. But people loved her cakes, especially her pandan sponge cake, and soon friends of friends started asking to buy them.

Hoa decided to turn her hobby into a business. She created a page on social media and posted photos of her cakes every day. She took orders by message and delivered the cakes on her motorbike. In the first month, she sold about thirty cakes. By the end of the year, she was selling more than two hundred a month.

Running a business was not always easy. Hoa had to learn how to calculate her costs, set prices and manage her time. Some weeks she worked until midnight. Once, a customer complained because a cake arrived late for a birthday party. Hoa apologised, gave a full refund and changed her delivery system so it never happened again.

Last month, Hoa opened a small shop with two employees. She still bakes every morning, but now she also trains her staff and plans new products. “My advice is simple,” she says. “Start small, listen to your customers and never stop learning.”

title: The Four-Day Week: Productivity or Fantasy?
summaryVi: Bài phân tích ưu và nhược điểm của tuần làm việc bốn ngày: nhân viên tập trung, ít kiệt sức hơn, nhưng không phù hợp với mọi ngành và kết quả có thể không bền vững.
body:
For more than a century, the five-day working week has been treated as a natural part of economic life. Recently, however, a growing number of companies have begun to experiment with a radical alternative: a four-day week with no reduction in pay. Supporters claim it makes employees happier without harming productivity. Critics argue that it is an idea that works well in a few offices but would be impractical across the wider economy.

The argument in favour rests on a simple observation: the number of hours people spend at work is not the same as the amount of useful work they do. Long meetings, constant email and simple tiredness all reduce efficiency. Companies that have tried a shorter week often report that staff become more focused, cutting unnecessary meetings and organising their time more carefully. Several trials have also reported lower rates of sickness and burnout, and some employers say the policy helps them to attract and keep talented workers in a competitive job market.

Yet the model is not suitable for every organisation. Hospitals, schools, shops and factories cannot simply close for an extra day; they would need to hire more staff or arrange complicated rotas, which increases costs. Even in office jobs, some employees report that squeezing five days of work into four makes each day more intense and stressful. There is also the question of whether early results will last. People who volunteer for a trial may be especially motivated, and productivity gains could fade once the novelty wears off.

Some businesses have chosen a middle path. Instead of a fixed day off for everyone, they offer flexible arrangements: compressed hours, a shorter Friday or a day off every other week. Others have concluded that the real lesson of the debate is not about the number of days at all, but about judging employees by their results rather than by how long they sit at their desks.

Whether or not the four-day week becomes standard, the discussion has forced many managers to reconsider assumptions that went unquestioned for generations. In that sense, it may already have changed the way we think about work.

title: Why We Put Things Off
summaryVi: Bài giải thích rằng trì hoãn chủ yếu là vấn đề cảm xúc chứ không phải quản lý thời gian, và gợi ý cách vượt qua: bắt đầu bằng bước rất nhỏ, loại bỏ xao nhãng, tha thứ cho bản thân.
body:
Almost everyone knows the feeling. You have an important task to do – an essay, a report, a difficult phone call – but instead of starting, you check your phone, tidy your desk or make another cup of tea. Hours later, the task is still waiting, and now you feel guilty as well. This habit of delaying things we know we should do is called procrastination.

Many people believe that procrastination is simply a sign of laziness or poor time management. However, psychologists increasingly see it as a problem with emotions rather than with time. When a task makes us feel anxious, bored or unsure of ourselves, avoiding it gives us immediate relief. The bad feelings disappear – at least for a while. Unfortunately, the task does not, and the stress usually comes back stronger than before.

Perfectionism can make the problem worse. If you believe your work must be perfect, starting it can feel frightening, because every first attempt is imperfect. Some people delay so that, if the result is poor, they can blame the lack of time rather than their ability.

So what can help? One useful strategy is to make the first step very small. Instead of “write my essay”, the goal becomes “write the first two sentences” or “work for ten minutes”. Once we start, continuing is often much easier. Another idea is to remove distractions, for example by putting your phone in another room. It also helps to be kind to yourself. Some research suggests that people who forgive themselves for procrastinating in the past are less likely to do it again, because they feel less negative about the task.

Procrastination is not a permanent character flaw. It is a habit, and like any habit, it can be understood and gradually changed.

title: Nobody Is Watching as Closely as You Think
summaryVi: “Hiệu ứng ánh đèn sân khấu” khiến ta nghĩ người khác chú ý đến mình nhiều hơn thực tế. Hiểu điều này giúp ta tự tin hơn, đặc biệt khi nói ngoại ngữ.
body:
Imagine arriving at a party and realising, too late, that you have a large coffee stain on your shirt. For the rest of the evening, you feel as though everyone is staring at it. In reality, it is quite likely that most of the guests never noticed. Psychologists have a name for this common experience: the spotlight effect.

The spotlight effect is our tendency to overestimate how much other people notice our appearance and behaviour. Because we experience the world from inside our own heads, we are intensely aware of our own mistakes, clothes and awkward moments, and it is easy to assume that others are equally focused on them. In fact, other people are mostly busy thinking about themselves – and, quite possibly, worrying about how they look to us.

In one well-known type of experiment, researchers asked students to walk into a room wearing a T-shirt that they found embarrassing. Afterwards, the students were asked to guess how many people in the room had noticed the shirt. Their estimates were typically far higher than the real number. Similar results have been found for bad hair days and for mistakes in presentations. Interestingly, the effect also applies to good performances: people rarely notice our successes as much as we expect, either.

A related idea is the “illusion of transparency” – the belief that our inner feelings are obvious to others. A speaker who feels nervous may be convinced that the audience can see her hands shaking or hear her voice trembling, when in fact she appears calm. Studies have suggested that simply telling speakers about this illusion can help them perform better, because it reduces their anxiety.

Understanding the spotlight effect can be surprisingly liberating. If people are paying less attention to us than we think, then a minor error in a meeting or an imperfect accent in a foreign language is unlikely to be remembered for long. For language learners, this matters: the fear of looking foolish often prevents people from speaking at all, yet the listener is usually far more interested in understanding the message than in judging the speaker.

This does not mean that our behaviour has no effect on others. But it does suggest that the harsh audience we imagine is, for the most part, an invention of our own minds.

title: Is It Still the Same Ship?
summaryVi: Câu đố “Con tàu của Theseus”: nếu thay từng tấm ván của một con tàu, nó còn là con tàu cũ không? Bài liên hệ câu hỏi này với bản thân con người.
body:
Imagine a famous wooden ship kept in a harbour as a museum piece. Over the years, its old planks begin to rot, so workers replace them one at a time with new wood. Eventually, after many decades, every single plank has been replaced. Is it still the same ship?

This puzzle is known as the Ship of Theseus, named after a hero from ancient Greek legend. Philosophers have discussed it for more than two thousand years, because it raises a deep question: what makes something the same thing over time?

Many people's first answer is “Yes, it's the same ship.” It has the same name and the same shape, and it sits in the same place. The changes happened slowly, so there was never a moment when the ship clearly stopped being itself. Others answer “No”. If none of the original material remains, they say, then what we have is a perfect copy, not the original.

The puzzle becomes even harder with an extra twist. Suppose someone collected all the old planks as they were removed and later used them to build a second ship. Now there are two ships. Which one is the real Ship of Theseus – the one in the harbour, or the one made from the original wood?

The question is not only about ships. Our bodies constantly replace their cells, and our opinions, memories and personalities change as we grow older. Are you the same person you were at five years old? Most of us would say yes, but it is surprisingly hard to explain exactly why.

There is no single correct answer. The value of the puzzle is that it makes us think carefully about words such as “same”, “identity” and “change” – words that we use every day without noticing how complicated they are.

title: Luck and Responsibility
summaryVi: Bài bàn về “may rủi đạo đức”: hai người có cùng hành vi nhưng kết quả khác nhau vì may rủi – có nên đánh giá họ khác nhau không? Bài trình bày ba cách trả lời của các triết gia.
body:
Two friends spend an evening at the same restaurant, drink the same modest amount of wine and decide, unwisely, to drive home. Both drive with the same degree of care. On the first friend's route nothing happens; he arrives home and goes to bed. On the second friend's route a child suddenly runs into the road and is seriously injured. The second driver will face criminal charges, public condemnation and, very likely, years of guilt. The first will probably have forgotten the evening within a week.

Most of us feel that the second driver has done something far worse. Yet when we try to justify that feeling, we run into difficulty. The two drivers made identical decisions and showed identical carelessness; the only difference lay in circumstances that neither of them controlled. If moral judgement should depend only on what is within a person's control – a principle that many people find intuitively compelling – then the two friends deserve exactly the same blame. Philosophers call this tension the problem of “moral luck”.

The problem extends well beyond road accidents. Consider how much of a person's character is shaped by factors they never chose: their genes, their upbringing, the culture and historical period into which they were born. Someone who lives a blameless life in peaceful times might, in a different era, have been drawn into terrible acts. If we are responsible only for what we control, and we control remarkably little, the space for genuine responsibility appears to shrink almost to nothing.

Several responses have been proposed. One is to bite the bullet and insist that the two drivers really are equally blameworthy, and that our instinct to blame the unlucky one more is simply a bias. On this view, the law may reasonably respond to outcomes for practical reasons, but morality should look only at intentions and choices. A second response accepts that luck does affect moral standing and argues that this is simply part of acting in an unpredictable world: when we act, we take responsibility not merely for our intentions but for what we actually bring about.

A third, more modest position suggests that we use the word “blame” in more than one sense. We can assess the quality of a person's decision, which is the same for both drivers, while also recognising that one of them stands in a uniquely painful relationship to a harm that actually occurred. The guilt of the second driver, on this account, is not irrational; it is a fitting response to having been the cause of suffering, even if the decision itself was no worse.

None of these answers fully dissolves the puzzle. But reflecting on moral luck can make us more cautious in our judgements of others, and perhaps more humble about our own good fortune.

The conflict between judging people only by what they control and our tendency to judge them by outcomes
The fact that drinking and driving is illegal

title: The Robot Who Wanted a Name
summaryVi: Một chú rô-bốt nhỏ giúp việc cho bà Green muốn có một cái tên. Nó chọn tên “Star” và rất hạnh phúc.
body:
In a small house at the end of a quiet street, there is a little robot. It is grey and blue, and it has two big round eyes. Every day, it cleans the floor, waters the plants and makes tea for an old woman called Mrs Green.

The robot is happy, but it has one problem. It does not have a name. Mrs Green calls it “Robot”. The cat calls it nothing, because cats do not talk.

One evening, the robot asks, “Mrs Green, can I have a name, please?” Mrs Green puts down her book. She looks at the robot for a long time. “Of course,” she says. “What name do you like?”

The robot thinks. It likes the sky. It likes the colour blue. It likes the small bright stars at night. “I like Star,” it says.

Mrs Green smiles. “Hello, Star,” she says. “Thank you for my tea.” Star's eyes shine very brightly. It is the best day of its life.

title: The Map in the Old Dictionary
summaryVi: Nam tìm thấy một tấm bản đồ cũ trong cuốn từ điển của ông. Hai ông cháu đi tìm và đào được chiếc hộp kim loại mà ông chôn từ hồi mười tuổi.
body:
Nam found the map on a rainy Sunday afternoon. He was looking for something to read on his grandfather's bookshelf when a thin piece of yellow paper fell out of an old dictionary. On the paper, someone had drawn a river, a bridge, three tall trees and a small red cross.

“Grandpa, what's this?” Nam asked. His grandfather put on his glasses and looked at the map for a long time. Then he laughed. “I drew that when I was ten years old,” he said. “I buried something under those trees. I forgot all about it!”

“What did you bury?” Nam asked excitedly. But his grandfather only smiled. “Why don't you find out?”

The next morning, the sun was shining. Nam and his grandfather walked along the river until they reached an old stone bridge. Not far away were three tall trees, exactly like the ones on the map. Nam started to dig with a small spade. After twenty minutes, he hit something hard. It was a metal box, brown with rust.

Inside, there was a toy car, a few old coins and a letter. The letter said: “To whoever finds this – I hope you are happy, and I hope you have a good friend to share adventures with.”

Nam looked at his grandfather and smiled. “I do,” he said.
